newsitem.title: UK: U.S. now seen holding key to U.N.'s future.
newsitem.headline: U.S. now seen holding key to U.N.'s future.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent

The United States holds the key to the success or failure of the United Nations now that the battle over who should be the next U.N. secretary-general is finished, European diplomats and analysts say.

Ghana's Kofi Annan, a career U.N. official who is well respected, may help push through some reforms while improving the atmosphere of gloom and stagnation that has plagued the 185-nation organisation as it approaches the 21st century.

But real decisions and power lie with the member nations -- above all with the United States, which has so far failed to pay huge debts and vetoed current U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali's bid for a second five-year term.

Diplomats say Washington's jaundiced view of the United Nations, particularly during President Bill Clinton's recent election campaign, has alienated European allies and offended much of the developing world.
"There is no doubt that we will be looking to the United States to repair some of that damage," said one European diplomat, who asked not to be identified.
"The Americans will be under tremendous pressure in 1997 to pay what they owe and to stop using the U.N. as a scapegoat."

Washington owes the United Nations some $1.3 billion, more than half of the total debt owed by member states. U.S. support, military and financial, is crucial to the success of U.N. peacekeeping and humanitarian operations around the world.
U.N. officials say the failure of some of those operations, particularly in Somalia and Bosnia, was unfairly blamed on them by the United States and others.
"If Annan can help break the funding logjam with the United States, then there won't be much longer-term damage to the U.N.," said Trevor Findlay of the Stockholm Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
"If that can't be done and the Americans don't pay up, then the picture looks very different."
Emma Matanle of the Royal Institute for International Affairs (RIIA) in London agreed.
"The fate of the United Nations lies in the hands of the U.S. Congress," she told Reuters.

"We can expect a lot of pressure on the Americans and they will have to do something, otherwise people will lose faith in the system. Complete domination by one country is not supposed to be what the United Nations is about."

Despite pressure from other members of the U.N. Security Council and particularly from France, the United States insisted on vetoing Boutros-Ghali for a second term, saying he had not done enough to carry out reforms and cut waste.
European allies and others feel that the United States, having won that battle, should now offer something in return.

Annan, who is respected in Washington and has said he will speak to the U.S. Congress on the issue if necessary, may help get the funds and thereby help move along other key issues of U.N. reform that have made little progress.

After being appointed on Tuesday by the U.N. General Assembly in New York, Annan pledged to make the organisation "leaner, more efficient and more effective" -- language that would please the United States in particular.
But he also urged member states not to destroy the United Nations through "financial starvation". Others used the occasion to make the point even more forcefully.
"Now that a new secretary-general is being appointed, all arrears should be paid at once, as has been promised so often in the past few months," said Boutros-Ghali.
Malaysia's Razali Ismail, president of the U.N. General Assembly president, said:
"The United Nations should not be donor driven...the secretary-general should not have to pose as a mendicant, petitioning government and legislatures alike, at the expense of all else."
The U.S. administration has been embarrassed by the criticism from its partners and is now worried about losing influence at the United Nations.
Princeton Lyman, Acting U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for International Organisation Affairs, said plans were being drafted so that Congress could agree to pay off the U.N. debt.
Lyman acknowledged there was "a great deal of resentment and anger" among other U.N. members over the issue.
"If we don't deal with this effectively in the next year or so, we're going to find it very difficult to mobilise votes in support of the things we need in the United Nations..." he said.
